title: Parvati's grief
hook: Shiva meets the boy at his own door; Parvati's grief, the Goddess's power, stops the universe
tomorrow: Shiva has to bring the boy back. so where does he find a head?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy made of earth, set at his mother's door with one job. The holy can live in clay. Today someone walks up to that door.

Here's a comment you might see under a video of a Ganesha festival: wait, his own dad cut his head off? Fair question, and the story has an answer. Why would a story like that be told at a festival full of kids? Start where it starts. Shiva walks home up the mountain to his own house, and at his own door is a boy he has never seen. You can't come in, says the boy. This is my house, says Shiva. My mother said no one. Shiva sends his ganas. The boy beats them back. In the Shiva Purana, even the gods can't get past him. Then Shiva raises his trident.
screen: `WAIT, HIS OWN DAD?` → `A STRANGER AT HIS OWN DOOR.` → `THE BOY SAYS NO.` → `THE TRIDENT.`

segments.voice: So, the puzzle. The story doesn't make anyone the villain. The boy is keeping his word to his mother. Shiva is trying to walk into his own home. Both are right, and something terrible happens anyway. Then Parvati comes out. In the Shiva Purana her grief is so big that she calls up fierce goddesses, forms of her own power, and sends them to swallow the universe. Narada and the gods come pleading, and she names her terms: bring my son back, and honor him among you. And Shiva, the great god, does what she asks. Here's the teaching. In Hinduism, God isn't only Father. God is also Mother, and her name is Shakti: power, the energy that moves everything. Parvati is one face of her; Durga and Kali, with their weapons, are others. Many Hindus pray to her simply as Ma. A saying many know plays on the letters: take the i of Shakti out of Shiva, and you get shava, a corpse. The god and his power can't be pulled apart. Nobody tells this mother to calm down. Her grief is the power of the universe, and even Shiva answers it. That's why a story like this can be told at a festival full of kids: it's a mother's love, bringing her child home.
screen: `BOTH OF THEM ARE RIGHT.` · `HER GRIEF STOPS THE UNIVERSE.` · `SHAKTI: GOD AS MOTHER, GOD AS POWER.` · `SHIVA WITHOUT SHAKTI: SHAVA.` · then, large: `GOD IS ALSO MOTHER: SHAKTI.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, bring to mind the strongest woman you know, the one whose care held your world together: a mother, a grandmother, an aunt, a teacher. Many Hindus pray to the Goddess with one word, Ma, said softly on the out-breath; if you pray, try it. If you don't, say her name instead, with a quiet thank you.
Trident: Shiva's three-pointed spear, trishula in Sanskrit, three spears. Raised at a door, it set off a grief even Shiva had to answer.
Hold onto this one: God is also Mother, and her name is Shakti. Even Shiva answers her. Day twenty-three, done.

screen: `DAY 23 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHERE DOES HE FIND A HEAD?`

howItsDone: Many Hindus worship God as the Mother, Shakti, in forms like Parvati, Durga and Kali, and call on her simply as Ma. This story is told as part of Ganesha's birth, often at Ganesh Chaturthi.

Shiva.meaning: the great god, honored as the one who destroys so things begin again

Parvati.meaning: the goddess who lives with Shiva; the boy's mother

ganas.meaning: Shiva's attendants, who guard his house

Narada.meaning: a sage who pleads with Parvati alongside the gods

Shakti.meaning: the Goddess as power: the energy that moves everything

Durga.meaning: a warrior form of the Goddess, who rides a lion

Kali.meaning: a fierce form of the Goddess
